extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, public relations professionals, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for identifying and selecting newsworthy stories using established 'news values' (criteria such as impact, timeliness, prominence, proximity, conflict, unexpectedness, currency and human interest). Useful for journalists, editors and PR professionals pitching stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies the number of people affected by a story; the more people involved or affected, the more newsworthy the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include large protests, mass accidents, or policy changes affecting many households. Everyday issues such as health, welfare, transport or national security also have big impact. The COVID‑19 pandemic is cited as an example of very high impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that happened recently are more newsworthy; what counts as 'recent' depends on the medium's publication cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television may treat events from the past half hour as timely, a monthly magazine may accept events within 30 days. Unfolding stories and breaking developments (especially on social media and 24‑hour news) have strong timeliness value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominent
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories involving well‑known people, places or companies attract attention and become news even when the action is trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Celebrities and politicians often generate coverage through their actions. Famous places or brand names similarly increase newsworthiness (example: a celebrity accident or a high‑profile politician’s mishap).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity / Closer to home
rubrics_metrics.description: Events occurring within the outlet’s circulation or broadcast area are more likely to be newsworthy; psychological closeness also matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local papers prioritize local redundancies or incidents over distant large events; stories involving locally known figures abroad will still be newsworthy for the home audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Events or situations where people or organisations are at odds (including violence, disputes, or tragedy) attract audience interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict adds drama which generates interest. Can range from terrorist attacks and murders to parliamentary disputes or celebrity fall‑outs. The adage 'if it bleeds it leads' is discussed as reflecting this value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected / Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that deviate sharply from expectations — surprising or bizarre occurrences — are likely to make news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes both hard‑news surprises (e.g., sudden capture of a leader) and bizarre/enteraining items (e.g., man biting dog, rare natural phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency / Trending stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that are already under public spotlight or are trending on social media are more newsworthy; topical fads and anniversaries also fit here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists can capitalise on social media trends (share counts, hashtags). Examples include extreme weather events trending globally, or mid‑season celebrity departures that dominate conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about people and events that stir emotions — personalised, emotive tales are appealing to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: dying child receiving an organ, families reuniting, or community reaction to tragedies. Everyday concerns like food, health, housing and schooling also have human‑interest pull.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity (Bad news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news — death, tragedy, disaster, failure — generally attracts more attention than good news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page notes many lists include negativity as a criterion. However journalists claim they choose stories for multiple news values, not negativity alone. Harcup & O'Neill list 'Bad news' separately as a value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity (Good news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive or 'feel‑good' stories can also be newsworthy and are recognised as a separate value by some modern lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harcup & O’Neill include 'Good news' and 'Entertainment' as values; outlets may balance bad and good news to avoid distorting public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The scale or size of an event must exceed a threshold to be recorded; larger scale increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threshold covers number affected, monetary scale, intensity or extremity (e.g., more gruesome crime or higher casualty accidents score higher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that occur suddenly and fit news schedules (one‑off incidents) are more newsworthy than slow, gradual trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: crashes, murders, plane crashes—because they fit production timetables. Long‑term trends are less likely to receive attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news tends to be more exciting and thus more likely to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlaps with general negativity; stories about violence, disaster, bankruptcy often rate higher and may also score on other values like unexpectedness or threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Unambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are easy to grasp and understand have higher news value; complex stories needing specialist knowledge may be ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, straightforward stories are preferred. Complexity reduces immediate newsworthiness unless simplified for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Reference to people
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories centred on named individuals attract more attention than abstract social forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human‑scale narratives (e.g., an individual’s achievement) increase interest compared to faceless trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Meaningfulness (cultural proximity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the audience identifies with the topic culturally influences newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared language, values or cultural norms make stories feel relevant—e.g., US news perceived as more relevant in the UK than distant nations with low cultural proximity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Reference to elite nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Events involving global powers or influential countries receive preferential coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage favors nations that can exert global influence; which nations are considered 'elite' may vary by country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Reference to elite persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about important, powerful, famous or influential people get more coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage preference for figures whose actions have outsized influence (e.g., presidents, industry leaders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that match media expectations or preconceived angles are more likely to be covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists are more prepared for events that fit their expectations; editorial readiness increases the chance of reporting even if it seems less unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Running stories or topics already in the news maintain momentum and are likely to receive ongoing coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing news teams and resources keep follow‑up coverage flowing; once headline news, a story tends to stay visible for some time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors balance different types of coverage; a story’s prominence depends on both its own value and competing stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may drop foreign news to make space for important domestic stories; composition is therefore an editorial judgment about mix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Selection hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The more an event satisfies the twelve news values, the more likely it is to be registered as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a predictive principle from Galtung & Ruge used to rank potential items for prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Distortion hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Once selected, a news item’s newsworthiness will be accentuated according to its values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection may be followed by emphasis that magnifies perceived importance or drama of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galtung and Ruge — Replication hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection and distortion processes occur at all steps from event to reader (reporting chain replication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News values influence not only initial selection but how the story is retold and framed across media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories exclusive to the news organisation (via interviews, surveys, polls, leaked documents) are valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unique access or proprietary content increases prominence and competitive advantage for an outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Bad news
rubrics_metrics.description: Reiterates that bad news remains a key contemporary value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad news is included alongside other factors; the authors note changes in balance due to celebrity interest and digital dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict remains an important contemporary value (see general 'Conflict').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as part of a modern checklist alongside exclusivity and shareability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprising or unexpected stories continue to be a driver of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely related to unexpectedness; used to capture items that deviate from norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Audio‑visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that offer arresting pictures or audio‑visual material have higher value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television and online platforms prize striking imagery; visuals increase shareability and audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: Likelihood that a story will be shared on social media increases its news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social media trends, memes and platform engagement now influence editorial choices; shareability can elevate otherwise niche items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with entertainment value are treated as a separate criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabloid or lightweight features may score highly on entertainment, attracting large audiences despite low 'hard news' value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Dramatic content
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic or sensational elements in a story increase its attractiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama can be manufactured by angle selection and emphasis; editors may favour stories that provide dramatic narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Follow‑up stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that lend themselves to follow‑ups (ongoing coverage) have extra value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors like stories that can be revisited over time, providing continuity and ongoing audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — The power elite
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about powerful people or institutions (the power elite) are prioritized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlap with 'reference to elite persons/nations'—focus on elites whose actions affect wider audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Relevance to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct relevance to the news organisation’s target audience increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlets set agendas with particular audiences in mind; what matters to one readership may be irrelevant to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Magnitude or impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The size or magnitude of an event is reaffirmed as a news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to 'Impact' and 'Threshold'—greater magnitude raises prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — Celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrity interest is a distinct contemporary news value driving coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growing public focus on celebrities changes what editors select; celebrity stories can cross entertainment and hard news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — News organisation’s own agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: An outlet’s internal agenda (political persuasion, style, ethos) shapes selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and owners influence the news agenda; stories are selected to fit institutional priorities and target audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead paragraph (lead) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead paragraph should summarise the whole story and answer the basic questions: who, what, where, when, why and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead usually shares the story’s main news values; it should contain the gist so readers can grasp the story quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline functions and criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A headline must catch the eye, grab attention, help readers select stories, and generally reflect the story while sometimes withholding detail to arouse curiosity; it should also consider keywords for search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines should balance attention‑grabbing with accurate reflection of the story. Since search engines matter, include relevant keywords while avoiding misleading sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple news values increase newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that satisfy several news values simultaneously are more likely to be prominent or lead stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the COVID pandemic or the Ukraine war which satisfy impact, timeliness, conflict, prominence, proximity, human interest and unexpectedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience perception and identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience preferences and identification influence news selection; audiences signal interest through circulation and viewing figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different audience members have differing interests; social media and citizen journalism blur lines between journalist and audience, enabling audiences to help define newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors, owners and senior journalists (gatekeepers) determine the news agenda by deciding which stories to run and how to frame them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gatekeeping occurs at many levels; reporters also exercise judgment about whom to interview and which parts of replies to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology and immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital technologies increase the importance of immediacy and timeliness; citizen journalism and mobile reporting alter what can be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mobile phones, social media and instant sharing shorten news cycles; outlets prioritise being first and may prefer shorter stories for audience consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values as ethical standards (editorial values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some organisations treat 'news values' as ethical or editorial principles (e.g., Associated Press, BBC Editorial Values) to guide responsible journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These editorial value statements spell out standards of behaviour and integrity for journalists (distinct from selection criteria) and aim to improve reliability and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for bad‑news interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A bad news story is of interest if it is out of the ordinary, makes considerable impact, is easy to grasp, and is meaningful/readily identified with by the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This summarises conditions under which negative stories become especially newsworthy, stressing understandability and audience identification alongside impact.
